newsitem.title: UK: UK stocks drop as rate fears shake Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: UK stocks drop as rate fears shake Wall Street.

text.p: UK shares fell on Friday as stronger-than-expected U.S. jobs data sent U.S. stocks and bonds sharply lower amid fresh fears of a rise in U.S. interest rates.
The FTSE 100 ended 30.4 points lower at 4,056.6, its lowest close for three weeks, led by retailers as a profit warning by Argos added to sector woes. Decliners led gainers three-to-one.

Stocks ended off the day's lows as the Dow rallied from an initial tumble of more than 50 points, to be down just 28 points as London closed. Yet with the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond down well over a full point, traders and strategists said the near-term UK outlook was mixed at best.

"The nonfarm payrolls were a bit of a shock," said a senior sales trader, adding that fears of UK interest rate rise coupled with recent downgrades on UK company earnings because of sterling strength made for a gloomy outlook for the UK market.
"It all means we are in turbulent waters and for the short term the market is probably going down...buyers can afford to stand back and pick their moment."

U.S. December nonfarm payrolls rose 262,000, compared with a an expected rise of 192,000, and the previous two month's figures were revised upwards. Average weekly hours and average hourly earnings also rose sharply.
BZW strategist Steve Wright said he expected a weak performance by UK shares in the first half of the year. "We are a bit bearish on the short-term outlook," Wright said.

"We are getting negative earnings news, we are unlikley to see great support from international markets with the Dow recently at record highs and there is concern over interest rate policy before the election."
"Europe is getting expensive. There is relative value in the UK but we felt the UK is unlikely to perform until after the election."
International stocks such as ICI, Zeneca and BOC bore the brunt of the day's selling after analysts this week cut earnings expectations due to sterling strength.
Yet banks extended recent gains on positive analyst comment and utilities rose on "safe haven" buying for their high yields and domestic exposure.

With their higher domestic presence, second-line stocks were spared the worst of the day's losses and the FTSE Mid 250 index fell just 9.9 points to 4,507.8. The Reuters-HSBC index of the top 150 stocks closed down 7.93 points at 1,098.92. Overall trading volume was busy at 952 million by 1702 GMT.

Ian Scott, strategist at Lehman Brothers, said fears over higher UK interest rates may have been overdone and sterling may be near its peak, yet the UK market would not be immune to jitters on Wall Street and in other world markets.
"We are fairly bullish on the UK but at this stage it looks as if we may outperform on the way down," Scott said.
From the start of trading today a profits warning from catalogue retailer Argos Plc helped snuff out an early FTSE advance. "The Argos statement really knocked sentiment," one senior dealer said.

A mixed distributive trades survey from the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) added to the gloom in the retail sector, with the CBI reporting that clothing, footwear, drugstores and durable goods retailers had a poor December.
Argos closed down 108p at 625 while elsewhere in the sector Next fell 23p to 528-1/2, Marks & Spencer 16-1/2p to 466 and GUS 22p to 580-1/2.
Top international stocks also continued to suffer from fears of earnings downgrades due to the persistent sterling strength, with ICI down 16-1/2p at 734-1/2 and BOC down 21-1/2p at 859-1/2.
Zeneca fell 42-1/2p to 15.95 stg.

Courtaulds Textiles bucked the market trend, rising 15-1/2p to 247p after predicting stronger profits for the second half of 1996, while Lloyds Chemists rose 14p to 526-1/2 after Germany's Gehe raised its takeover terms.

Tate & Lyle fell 16-1/2p to 468-1/2 as UBS cut earnings forcasts for the sugar producer while Barclays led banks higher, up 12p at 10.68-1/2, as Kleinwort Benson added the stock to its list of ten preferred stocks for the year ahead.
-- David Holmes, London Newsroom +44 171 542 5106
